title: CLAY COUNTY RACCOON ROUNDUP
full_story:
The Clay County Farm Bureau is launching a “Raccoon Roundup” program to combat rising property damage from an increased raccoon population.

The initiative offers a $3 cash reward per raccoon tail for Farm Bureau members during the upcoming Illinois hunting and trapping seasons.

Two collection events will take place at the Farm Bureau office in Louisville from 6:00 to 7:00 PM on November 12th and January 14th.

Participants are limited to 33 tails per collection date and must present a valid DNR hunting or trapping license.  All harvests must strictly follow state regulations.

title: IUKA MAN INJURED
full_story:
An Iuka man was injured Saturday night in a single-vehicle crash on the Omega Road.

According to the Marion County Sheriff’s Department, 54-year-old Joseph Grear was driving near the entrance to Forbes State Park around 6:15 pm when his car left the roadway and struck a tree.

Deputies report Grear was able to get out of the vehicle on his own.  He was treated at the scene and transported by United Medical Response to Salem Township Hospital for further evaluation.

title: TWO MEN IN CUSTODY
full_story:
The Marion County Sheriff’s Department reports that deputies responded to a burglary in progress on South College Street in Salem.  After suspects refused to come out, deputies and a Centralia Police K-9 unit forced their way through a barricaded door.

Centralia Police K-9 “Ace” successfully apprehended 45-year-old David Linder of Iuka, who required medical treatment for injuries sustained during the arrest.  The second suspect, 32-year-old Jubal Dulaney of Salem, was discovered hiding in the attic using a thermal imaging camera.

Sheriff Kevin Cripps says both men face charges of criminal trespass and resisting arrest.  While initially reported as a burglary, investigators believe Linder and Dulaney had been squatting in the home.  Authorities are still investigating whether the men stole items or were attempting to strip wiring from the property.

Sheriff Cripps commended the responding deputies and extended a special thanks to the Centralia Police Department and K-9 Ace for bringing the incident to a safe conclusion.

title: OCC SCIENCE LABS OPEN HOUSE
full_story:
Olney Central College is getting ready to pull back the curtain on a massive upgrade to its campus.

This Tuesday, the college will host a public open house to showcase its newly renovated science labs inside the Dr. Kent L. Wattleworth Hall.  The extensive two-million-dollar project marks the first major overhaul for the third-floor physics, chemistry, and biology facilities since the building first opened in 1974.

School officials say the summer-long renovations replaced obsolete workspaces with modern, high-tech environments.  Faculty members note that the upgrades don’t just solve decades-old infrastructure problems like plumbing leaks and power outages, they also introduce advanced safety equipment, dual chemical hoods, and a dedicated space for the college’s anatomy cadaver.

OCC President Chris Simpson says the new facilities will drastically enhance student success, giving them access to undergraduate research projects that rival major universities.

The project was heavily backed by the OCC Foundation, which contributed thousands of dollars in equipment, including a new ten-thousand-dollar water purification system.

The open house runs tomorrow from 4:00 to 6:00 pm, and community members, alumni, and prospective students are all invited to attend.

title: COMPUTERS FOR BEGINNERS CLASSES
full_story:

title: IFB URGES DYED DIESEL DOCUMENTATION
full_story:
Illinois drivers considering the temporary use of red-dyed diesel on roads received additional clarity from the Illinois Department of Revenue (IDOR) and the IRS.

The IRS announced October 14th that it will not impose penalties when dyed diesel fuel is sold for use or used on highways nationwide through December 31st in response to President Donald Trump’s October 5th executive order on diesel fuel cost relief.

The IRS guidance also states they anticipate issuing further guidance as to the postponement of payment of taxes imposed and will continue to explore ways to eliminate the obligation to pay any amounts deferred.  IFB reminds members this temporary relief does not permanently eliminate fuel tax obligations, it only defers them to a later time.

While the IRS said taxpayers do not need to maintain records to substantiate eligibility for the federal relief, the federal directive does not override requirements established under Governor JB Pritzker’s October 6th executive order and subsequent IDOR guidance.

“Illinois documentation requirements remain in effect,” IFB said in guidance distributed to members.  The organization emphasized that members seeking Illinois penalty relief must continue maintaining documentation for qualifying agricultural transportation conducted between October 6th and December 31st and retain those records for four years.

In response to high diesel prices, Pritzker directed IDOR and Illinois State Police to not impose a penalty when dyed diesel fuel from bulk storage is sold or used on highway or state roads for agricultural purposes through the end of the year.

Red-dyed diesel is standard diesel fuel marked with a red dye to indicate it is tax‑exempt and legally restricted to off‑road use such as farming, construction, generators and marine/rail equipment.  It is chemically the same as clear on‑road diesel but sold without highway fuel taxes.

Additional questions can be directed to IFB Associate Director of Transportation and Infrastructure Rodney Knittel at 309-557-3662 or [email protected].
